title: Wage theft: when pay is delayed or withheld
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Delayed or withheld pay is workers' commonest complaint. What the Code on Wages says on timing, deductions and penalties, and the practical steps to take.
body:
For many workers, the biggest hardship is not low pay. It is pay that arrives late, arrives in part, or does not arrive at all. A worker lives from one payday to the next. Rent, school fees, the milk bill and the instalment on a loan all fall due on fixed dates, and a delay of even a week can push a family into borrowing at ruinous interest. This post explains what the law now says about the time and manner of payment, what a worker can do when wages are withheld, and why this issue is so often the first one a union takes up.

## What the Code on Wages says about timing

The **Code on Wages, 2019** is one of the four Labour Codes brought into effect on 21 November 2025. Section 17 of the Code lays down when wages must be paid:

- **Daily-rated workers:** at the end of the shift.
- **Weekly:** on the last working day of the week, before the weekly holiday.
- **Fortnightly:** before the end of the second day after the fortnight ends.
- **Monthly:** before the expiry of the seventh day of the following month.
- **On separation:** if a worker is removed, dismissed, retrenched or resigns, or becomes unemployed because the establishment closes, wages are to be paid within **two working days** of that event.

The appropriate Government may fix a different reasonable time limit, and nothing in the section overrides a payment deadline fixed by another law. A commentary on the Code notes that the wage period cannot be longer than one month and that the Code's timely-payment and deduction protections now cover all employees, not only those below a wage ceiling, as under the older Payment of Wages Act, 1936.

Readers may find it interesting that in 1944, when Dr Ambedkar was Labour Member, he argued against the different payment deadlines that applied to larger and smaller factories and proposed one uniform deadline of seven days. The principle of a clear, short, uniform deadline is an old demand of the labour movement.

## Deductions

An employer cannot simply cut a worker's pay. The Code allows deductions only for authorised reasons, such as fines or damages for specified acts, recoveries of advances and certain statutory payments. Summaries of the Code state that **total deductions in any wage period cannot exceed 50 percent of wages**. The Code's rules require the employer to give a **wage slip** on or before the payment date, in physical or electronic form, so that the worker can see what was paid and what was deducted. A worker who is handed cash with no slip has no record, and a worker with no record has no case.

## Minimum wages, floor wage, overtime and bonus

Timely payment is only worth as much as the wage that is paid. Under the Code, as the Labour Ministry's summary notes, minimum wages apply to all workers and not only to those in scheduled employments, and a **national floor wage** is to ensure a minimum living standard, below which no State may fix its minimum wage. Overtime is to be paid at not less than twice the ordinary rate, and with consent. The Code on Wages also covers statutory bonus in establishments with 20 or more employees, where employees up to the prescribed wage limit are eligible for a bonus of between 8.33 and 20 percent of wages, payable within eight months of the close of the accounting year. A summary of the sector provisions adds that salaries in IT and ITES establishments are to be paid by the seventh of each month.

## What to do if wages are withheld

The Code establishes both advice and enforcement. A new kind of officer, the **Inspector-cum-Facilitator**, replaces the traditional inspector, with a duty to advise employers on compliance as well as to inspect and prosecute. Employees can file claims for delayed wages or unauthorised deductions before the authority appointed under the Code, within the time limit the Code and its rules prescribe, and can approach civil courts in some cases. For a migrant worker, the Labour Ministry's summary notes that claims for pending dues can be raised for up to three years.

A practical sequence is:

1. **Keep proof of work.** Attendance records, messages, photographs of duty rosters, wage slips, bank statements and the name of the supervisor all matter. If there is no appointment letter, ask for one: the Codes make appointment letters mandatory for all workers.
2. **Send a written demand** to the employer, giving the period, the amount due and a reasonable date for payment. Keep a copy, and if possible send it by a method that creates a record.
3. **Approach your union.** A collective demand is often resolved faster than an individual one. In many BMS units, unpaid wages are the first item taken up in meetings with management and officials.
4. **Approach the labour department's inspector or the authority for claims.** Explain the facts, attach the records, and ask for the matter to be taken up with the employer and, in the case of contract workers, with the principal employer.
5. **If the employer is a contractor,** remember that under the OSH Code the principal employer must pay the wages if the contractor does not, and may recover the amount from the contractor.

## Penalties

The Code provides penalties for non-payment or underpayment of wages. A summary of its provisions mentions a fine of up to ₹50,000 for a first offence and, for a repeat offence within five years, imprisonment of up to three months, a fine of up to ₹1,00,000, or both, with some first offences compoundable. Penalties are not the main objective. The aim of the Code's facilitative approach is to bring the employer into compliance before the dispute escalates, but a union can insist that the law is not treated as optional.

## Where the problem is worst

Delayed or withheld pay is reported across the economy, and particularly in:

- **construction**, where payments pass through several layers of contractors;
- **domestic work**, where there is no written contract and often no witness;
- **security services**, where agencies delay payment of guards who cannot leave their posts;
- **contract work** in factories, ports and public offices; and
- **small units**, where a single delayed payment from a customer can trigger delays all the way down the chain.

Public sector undertakings are not exempt. In its call for a nationwide Protest Day on 25 February 2026, BMS pointed to National Textile Corporation mills in eight States that had paid only 50 percent of wages since the pandemic, with salaries pending for ten months, and to workers of the Heavy Engineering Corporation in Ranchi who had gone 32 months without salary. It asked that wage dues in PSUs such as NTC mills, HEC, ITI and HMT be paid. These are long delays, and they show that the problem is not confined to small private employers.

## What BMS asks

BMS has asked for strict, universal enforcement of labour laws, with accountability for principal employers, and for the tripartite machinery, meaning the Government, employers and unions, to be convened regularly so that systemic problems such as wage arrears in public enterprises can be raised and resolved. At its Puri conference it resolved that labour laws must apply to all workers without exclusion, which for wage claims means that a contract worker, a domestic worker and a home-based worker should have the same right to timely pay as a permanent factory employee.

## For employers

Pay on time. If cash flow is difficult, tell the workers and agree a date in writing rather than letting the delay stretch silently. Issue wage slips, maintain registers, and pay contractors promptly so that they can pay the workers. A day's delay for the employer is a month's difficulty for the worker.
